articles.title: Howard Lutnick has been Trump’s ally for decades. His ties to Nvidia may spell his downfall
articles.summary: Billionaire commerce secretary faces scrutiny after sex scandal reveals his role in sales of chips to China. Howard Lutnick, the beleaguered US commerce secretary and close ally of Donald Trump, is emerging as Democrats’ prime target when the party takes control of Congress in January.
body: Lutnick is resisting calls to resign amid a bipartisan outcry over his role in the scandal at artificial intelligence (AI) company Nvidia and the sale of microchips to China, the US’s principal geopolitical rival in the race for AI supremacy.

The 65-year-old billionaire received a vote of confidence from Trump on Friday but faces growing criticism from some Republicans and a chorus of Democrats vowing to investigate his actions and demanding that he testify on Capitol Hill. Among their questions is whether Lutnick compromised national security to make money for his family.

Although cabinet members such as the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, have faced calls for accountability, Lutnick is now in the sights of a newly emboldened Congress eager to bring the Trump administration to book.

articles.title: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.summary: Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument. The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons…
body: The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.

Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.

“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.

articles.title: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
articles.summary: Major US financial institutions are banning third-party bots from logging into your accounts—and warning that any costly bot mistakes are strictly your problem.
body: Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

articles.title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
articles.summary: Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event. With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness.
body: On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.

Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.

articles.title: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die
articles.summary: Biologically important chemical reactions persisted in the sterilized soil for six years—offering clues to how life on Earth may have gotten its start.
body: For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration —to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.
points: Biologically important chemical reactions persisted in the sterilized soil for six years—offering clues to how life on Earth may have gotten its start.

articles.title: How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
articles.summary: While some regions get wetter, others face massive drought. On top of wars and cuts to foreign aid, the weather phenomenon could leave millions of people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat.
body: This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

articles.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
articles.summary: It's a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.
body: As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.

Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

articles.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
articles.summary: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called "killer robots." Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to "start discussing options" after a largely fruitless week of…
body: Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

articles.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
articles.summary: Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order.
body: Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.

Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.

Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.
